passage:
I live across the landing from Gurleen aunty, so I hear most mornings. 'Nikita, shoes! Nikita, where's your tie? Nikita, the van's here!' Then a door bangs and Nikita runs down, one sock in her hand.
Last week I met aunty on the stairs, eyes red. 'I love that girl so much,' she said. 'But by eight o'clock I'm already exhausted.'
Since then something has changed. I heard aunty say, 'Step one: shoes,' and wait. Then, 'Great, you did that fast! Step two: bag.' Shorter, calmer. She also told my mother she has joined a parents' group at Nikita's school on Saturdays. 'Just to talk to people who get it,' she said.
This morning Nikita came down with both socks on, grinning. Aunty was smiling too.

qa.q: What did Nikita have in her hand when she ran down?
qa.a: One sock.

qa.q: What did Gurleen aunty feel on the stairs, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt both deep love and exhaustion; her eyes were red and she said she loves Nikita but is worn out by eight.

qa.q: What changes did Gurleen aunty make, and why do they help?
qa.a: She gave short one-step instructions, praised Nikita's effort and joined a parents' group, which made mornings calmer and gave her support too.

qa.q: What might mornings feel like for Nikita now?
qa.a: Nikita may feel less rushed and more capable, getting one step at a time and praise instead of constant calling.

grounding: Shows, through a neighbour's eyes, a parent worn out by daily morning battles who feels love and exasperation, and who uses short instructions, praise and support.

passage:
Monday: By 7.40 Arohi had said 'Tushar, brush your teeth' five times. He was building a paper plane. She shouted, he cried, and they both left the flat angry. On the bus to work she stared out of the window, aching with love and frustration.
Thursday evening: She and Tushar drew a morning chart together: a toothbrush, a shirt, a bag, a shoe. 'You tick, I don't shout,' she said. She also called her sister and just talked for half an hour.
The next Monday: Tushar stood at the chart in his vest, ticking boxes. 'Look, Mumma, three already!' 'You're working hard,' Arohi said, and meant it. They left on time. He even had his plane.

qa.q: What was Tushar building instead of brushing his teeth?
qa.a: A paper plane.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling on the bus to work on Monday?
qa.a: She was aching with love and frustration after a morning of shouting and tears.

qa.q: What choices on Thursday made the next Monday calmer?
qa.a: Drawing a picture chart with Tushar so he could tick steps without her shouting, and calling her sister for support.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel ticking boxes on the chart?
qa.a: He may feel proud and in charge of his own morning, especially when Arohi says he's working hard.

grounding: Shows a parent exhausted by morning battles who feels both love and exasperation, and uses a clear chart, praise for effort and support for herself.

passage: Counsellor's note, parent meeting. Samir came in looking exhausted. He described mornings with his son Chinmay: ten reminders to brush his teeth, shoes found under the sofa, the school van honking while Chinmay builds a paper plane. "I love him so much," Samir said, "and by eight I'm shouting like someone I don't recognise." His eyes filled. We talked about short, one-step instructions, a picture checklist on the bathroom mirror, and praising Chinmay when he tries, even if the socks don't match. I also gave Samir the number of the parents' support group that meets on Saturdays; he said he hadn't thought he was allowed to need help. We will meet again in three weeks.

qa.q: Where will the picture checklist go?
qa.a: On the bathroom mirror.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Samir describe?
qa.a: Deep love for Chinmay and exhausted exasperation that leads to shouting.

qa.q: What supports did the counsellor suggest?
qa.a: One-step instructions, a picture checklist, praising effort and a parents' support group for Samir.

qa.q: How might Chinmay experience the mornings?
qa.a: Chinmay probably feels scolded and rushed, while his mind drifts to things like paper planes.

grounding: Shows a parent worn out by morning battles, feeling love and exasperation, and getting strategies and support for himself.

passage:
Thursday. This morning was a war. Divyansh lost his other shoe, then his tie, then his homework, and I heard myself screaming. He cried in the auto. I cried in the kitchen. I love this boy so much it hurts. He's funny, he's kind to his little cousin, he builds amazing things out of cardboard. But by 7.30 every day I'm empty. Tonight I tried what the teacher suggested: one instruction at a time. "Shoes by the door." Done. "Bag by the shoes." Done. I said, "You did both, well done," and he beamed like I'd given him a medal. And I've asked my sister to take the Saturday mornings so I can sleep in once a week.
Mahima

qa.q: What does Divyansh build out of cardboard?
qa.a: Amazing things.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel by 7.30 every morning?
qa.a: Mahima feels empty and worn out, even while loving Divyansh deeply.

qa.q: Which of Mahima's changes seem to help, and why?
qa.a: Short one-step instructions with praise, which made Divyansh beam, and asking Mahima's sister for help to get some rest.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel when praised?
qa.a: He beamed with pride, as if he had won a medal.

grounding: Illustrates a parent exhausted by daily battles who uses short instructions, praise and support to keep home warm.

passage: In their house at the edge of Barabanki, Usha had called Tanvir to the well six times. Each time he answered, "Coming, Ammi!" and each time something caught him: a kite, a line of ants, the neighbour's new calf. By the time he came, the bucket had tipped and the water had run into the dust. Usha sat down on the step, too tired to shout. She loved his bright chatter and hated the endless reminders. Then she remembered the health worker's advice at the women's group. She stood up, took Tanvir's hand and said just one thing: "Bucket. Now." He carried it. "Good, you did it," she said. He glowed. That evening she told the women's group how worn out she'd been, and they listened.

qa.q: How many times had Usha called Tanvir?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: How was Usha feeling as she sat on the step?
qa.a: She felt worn out and exasperated, while still loving his bright chatter.

qa.q: What worked better than calling from a distance?
qa.a: Taking his hand, giving one short instruction and praising him when he did it.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel when praised?
qa.a: He glowed with pride.

grounding: Shows a mother worn out by daily reminders, using clear short instructions, praise and her own support group.

passage:
Half past seven in their flat in Manchester, and Nkechi was saying "shoes" for the fifth time. Xin, nine, was lying on the hall floor reading the cereal box.
"Xin! Shoes! We are late again!" Her voice cracked. He jumped up, found one shoe, and forgot the other.
In the car, Nkechi gripped the wheel. She loved his quick jokes and his drawings of dragons. She was also so tired of mornings that she felt like crying.
That week she tried the ideas from the parents' support group at school: one short instruction at a time, a picture list by the door, and "Well done for getting your coat without me asking." On Thursday Xin found both shoes himself. Nkechi high-fived him, then texted the group, "Small win."

qa.q: Where was Xin lying at half past seven?
qa.a: He was lying on the hall floor reading the cereal box.

qa.q: How did Nkechi feel as she gripped the wheel in the car?
qa.a: She felt worn out and close to tears, yet still full of love for Xin's jokes and dragon drawings.

qa.q: What helped mornings go better for Nkechi and Xin?
qa.a: Short single instructions, a picture list, praise for effort and a support group for Nkechi herself made mornings calmer.

qa.q: What is it like for Xin when Nkechi shouts "Shoes!" again?
qa.a: He probably feels startled and flustered, rushing to obey and still forgetting the other shoe.

grounding: Nkechi, worn out by morning battles with her son, feels both love and exasperation and finds that short instructions, praise and support help.
